<!-- file: principles/authority.md -->

## Authority: which instruction wins

Motomation has many kinds of guidance. They are not equal. When two of them disagree, the higher level wins, and the plan says so in one line (`Conflict: <lower> yields to <higher>: <why>`). The most emphatic sentence never wins just by being emphatic.

| Level | What it is | Examples | Can be overridden by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Explicit user requirements and constraints** | what the user asked for, excluded or approved | "must have a cart", "no dark mode", "use our Vite app", an approved Scope row | only the user |
| **2. Safety, accessibility, correctness** | standards that protect people and keep the product working | WCAG 2.2 AA, keyboard and focus, reduced-motion paths, no fake claims, no copied protected work, security headers, licences | nothing in this skill; a user request that breaks one is raised, not silently obeyed |
| **3. Project architecture and technical constraints** | what the existing codebase, stack, runtime and budget allow | the project's framework, its component system, its package policy, performance budgets | levels 1–2 |
| **4. The product contract** | what this product must let people do, derived before any art direction (`thinking/product-contract.md`) | journeys, routes, required states, IA, information density | levels 1–3, or the user approving a scope change |
| **5. Research evidence** | what real products and references show for this project | type research, reference findings with their limitations | levels 1–4 |
| **6. Design heuristics and opinions** | the skill's taste, stated as advisory rules with rationale (`principles/heuristics.md`, `principles/house-style.md`, `principles/dials.md`) | one focal point per screen, one accent, a minimal nav | levels 1–5; ignoring one needs a one-line reason, not permission |
| **7. Recipes, archetypes, examples, components, draws** | starting material: `categories/`, `structures/`, `styles/`, `signatures/`, `examples/`, `data/`, `scripts/collide.mjs` | "Ledger" archetype, the ecommerce recipe, a library card component | everything above; a recipe that fights the contract is adapted or dropped |

### How to use the table

- **The product contract outranks every aesthetic idea.** A concept may reorganise how the product is presented. It may not remove a journey, hide an essential function or cut a required route to make the composition cleaner. If a concept only works without a required capability, the concept changes.
- **Heuristics guide; they don't decide.** Every opinion in this skill exists to solve a design problem (`principles/heuristics.md` names the problem). When the problem isn't present, the opinion doesn't apply. Following a heuristic that makes the product worse is a failure, not loyalty.
- **Recipes are evidence of one way it was done, never the answer.** The agent may discover a better solution than anything in the library; it is expected to look.
- **Measured gate checks are level 2 or 4.** The gate's hard checks (contrast, overflow, reduced motion, accessibility names, completeness X, journey J) protect people and the product, and they fail the build. The critique scores (H, R, S, V, M) are diagnostics at level 6: a low score asks a question, it does not override the contract (`gates/delivery-gate.md`, Part 4).
- **A user can lower level 6 or 7 at will** ("make it conventional"), and can change level 4 by approving a scope change. Nobody, including the agent, changes level 4 silently.

### Conflicts that come up often

| Conflict | Resolution |
|---|---|
| "Keep navigation minimal" vs a marketplace with 40 categories | the IA the product needs wins; restraint is applied to the nav's styling, not its contents |
| A signature move vs a dense task screen (checkout, dashboard) | the task screen stays conventional and fast; the signature lives where the product has room for it, or the site has none |
| Archetype draw vs the product's information architecture | the IA wins; the archetype may shape one storytelling surface or nothing |
| Memory says "diverge on all five" vs a brief that needs the same type mode as last time | diverge where the brief doesn't justify the similarity; never diverge into a worse fit, and say which similarity is justified |
| Banned display font vs a product whose brand system already uses it | the brand's existing system (level 1 or 3) wins; note it |
| Accent ≤ 5% vs a colour-coded product (transit lines, grocery categories, a kids' brand) | colour that carries information or brand is not "accent"; the contrast floor still holds |
| A backend deferred vs its interface | deferring payment, auth or search infrastructure never removes the screen; the interface ships, labelled as demo (`thinking/product-contract.md`) |


---

<!-- file: principles/color.md -->

## Colour

Colour in this house style is quiet by default and loud at one moment.

### Method

1. **Ground:** choose the background temperature from the concept (warm paper, cool concrete, dark room).
2. **Ink:** the text colour, never pure black on pure white unless starkness is the concept. Aim for 12:1 or higher contrast for body text on the ground.
3. **Muted:** a secondary text and hairline colour, at 4.5:1 or higher for any text.
4. **Accent:** one hue, chosen from the concept (safelight red for a darkroom, brass for a hotel, signal green for a terminal).
5. **Surface:** at most one extra tone for cards or panels, 3–6% away from the ground.

Search curated palettes with `node scripts/search.mjs palettes "<words from the brief>"` and verify every pair with `node scripts/contrast.mjs <fg> <bg>`.

### Tokens

```css
:root {
  --ground: #F3F0EA;
  --surface: #EAE6DE;
  --ink: #151412;
  --muted: #5E5A53;
  --line: color-mix(in oklab, var(--ink) 14%, transparent);
  --accent: #D9481E;
  --accent-ink: #FFFFFF;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { /* only if the concept supports both */ }
```

Use OKLCH or `color-mix(in oklab, …)` for tints so they stay perceptually even.

### Rules

- **Accent footprint ≤ 5% of any screen.** Reserve it for the action, the active state or the signature.
- **No default gradients.** If you use one, it must come from the concept (a sunset hotel, a heat map) and be built in OKLCH to avoid muddy middles.
- **Dark mode is a design, not an inversion.** Lower the contrast of large surfaces slightly, raise the accent's lightness, and swap shadows for hairlines.
- **Images set the palette.** When photography leads, sample the ground and accent from the photos.
- **Contrast is non-negotiable:** 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text (24px+, or 18.66px+ bold) and UI boundaries.


---

<!-- file: principles/dials.md -->

## The Three Dials

Every design sets three dials, each at **1, 2 or 3**. There are three levels, not ten, because a model and a reviewer can reliably tell calm from bold, but cannot reliably tell a 6 from a 7. Hold the dials across the site; a product may set them per route family (a store's launch story at MOTION 3, its checkout at MOTION 1), and says so.

| Dial | 1 (Calm) | 2 (Balanced) | 3 (Bold) | What it controls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ENERGY** | Still, lots of air | Confident, clear contrast | Loud, huge type, strong colour moments | Type scale jumps, contrast, accent strength |
| **RHYTHM** | Uniform, predictable sections | Consistent with deliberate breaks | Every section a different composition | Layout variation, grid breaks, asymmetry |
| **MOTION** | Hover/focus/press only | Reveals, pinned moments, kinetic type | Scroll-as-film, choreography, WebGL | Motion tier and quantity |

### Dials → motion tier

| MOTION dial | Default tier | Allowed range |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tier 1 | 1 |
| 2 | Tier 2 | 1–3 |
| 3 | Tier 2–3; Tier 5 for a chapter only when the story has media to scrub | 2–5 (Tier 4 only if the concept is spatial) |

### Where the settings come from

There are no presets. Each dial is set from the brief: what the visitor must do, how the brand should feel in the brief's own words, and what the concept needs. When a visual language helps, `styles/` is the reference: each row of `data/styles.csv` carries the energy, rhythm and motion that language usually runs at. Treat those as a starting point to argue with, not a value to copy.

Set dials directly with `--energy=3 --rhythm=2 --motion=3`.

### Levers (how dials become decisions)

- **A clear first read per screen.** On storytelling screens that is usually one focal point (H-focal); on dense product screens it is a reading order (title → controls → results).
- **Hierarchy by contrast:** size, weight and colour differ on purpose.
- **Whitespace as structure:** space groups and separates; it is not leftover.
- **Disciplined accent:** zero accents is sterile; accent everywhere is noise (H-one-accent). Colour that carries information or brand is not accent.
- **An identity motif:** a gesture, a shape, a typographic habit or a system quality (density, rhythm, precision) that repeats and makes the site belong to its brand.

### Example settings

- Motion designer portfolio: ENERGY 3 · RHYTHM 2 · MOTION 3
- Boutique hotel: ENERGY 1 · RHYTHM 2 · MOTION 2
- Developer tool: ENERGY 2 · RHYTHM 1 · MOTION 2
- Government service: ENERGY 1 · RHYTHM 1 · MOTION 1
- Music festival: ENERGY 3 · RHYTHM 3 · MOTION 3
- B2B procurement catalogue: ENERGY 1 · RHYTHM 1 · MOTION 1 (identity from type and density)
- General marketplace: ENERGY 2 · RHYTHM 1 · MOTION 1–2 (storytelling only on campaign surfaces)

These are illustrations. The brief, the contract and research set the dials; `principles/heuristics.md` → H-rhythm explains when RHYTHM 3 hurts.

<!-- file: principles/heuristics.md -->

## Heuristics: the skill's opinions, with their reasons

Every opinion in Motomation lives here, at authority level 6 (`principles/authority.md`). Each one names the problem it solves, where it applies, what it costs and when to ignore it. Other files point here instead of restating an opinion as a rule.

**How to use them.** Read the problem first. If the project has that problem, the heuristic is a good default; apply it or adapt it. If the project doesn't have that problem, skip it. Ignoring a heuristic needs a one-line reason in `DESIGN.md` under `Decision trace`; it never needs permission and is never a gate failure on its own.

A heuristic never overrides the product contract (level 4), research evidence (level 5) or anything above them.

### Composition and hierarchy

| ID | Heuristic | Problem it solves | Applies when | Trade-off | Ignore or adapt when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H-focal | One focal point per screen | pages where everything shouts and nothing is read first | marketing, editorial and storytelling screens | can starve dense screens of scannability | dashboards, catalogues, comparison tables, search results: there the hierarchy is a reading order (title → filters → results), not one focal point |
| H-grid-break | A deliberate grid break on a screen | a page that reads as a template because every block sits in the same columns | editorial, brand and portfolio pages with room to breathe | breaks cost scanning speed and responsive effort | task flows (checkout, forms, settings, data tables), where alignment is the usability |
| H-rhythm | Vary section compositions (RHYTHM dial) | long pages that repeat one block pattern | long scrolling narratives | variety for its own sake makes a product page feel incoherent | product listings, docs, dashboards: repeated structure is how users learn the page |
| H-centred-hero | Avoid the centred hero + subtitle + two buttons + screenshot | the most common AI template | when the concept has a better opening | a centred hero is sometimes the clearest answer | the product needs an immediate primary action (search box, booking widget, sign-up) and centring serves it; say why |
| H-bento | Avoid the bento grid and the three-icon feature row | generic SaaS sameness | when the content isn't actually a set of equal features | some content really is a set of equal items | the items are equal and comparable (pricing tiers, plan features, category tiles in a store) |

### Navigation and information architecture

| ID | Heuristic | Problem it solves | Applies when | Trade-off | Ignore or adapt when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H-nav-minimal | Minimal navigation (wordmark plus a few links) | portfolio and brand sites where the nav competes with the work | small sites, under ~8 destinations, low return-visit frequency | hides breadth; costs findability | marketplaces, publications, B2B catalogues, institutions, dashboards: the nav must expose the IA the product contract defines (categories, search, account, cart, mega-menu or sidebar). Restraint then applies to how the nav looks, not what it contains |
| H-nav-conventional | The "logo left, links centre, button right" nav reads as a template | default chrome on a brand site | brand, portfolio, campaign sites | the convention exists because people find things in it | any product where speed of wayfinding matters more than identity (commerce, SaaS app, booking, docs). Familiar is correct there; make it excellent instead of different |
| H-remove-expected | "Remove the expected" mutation (no nav, no hero image, no grid) | predictable structure | experimental and campaign pages | removing nav removes wayfinding | anything with more than one task, any product route, any mobile flow: never remove the nav, search, cart, account or primary action the contract requires |

### Type and colour

| ID | Heuristic | Problem it solves | Applies when | Trade-off | Ignore or adapt when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H-type-hero | Type as the image, display at 8–28vw (HOUSE STYLE) | weak, timid typographic identity | brand, editorial, portfolio, campaign | huge type pushes content below the fold; wraps badly at 375px | SERVICE STYLE products, imagery-led commerce, data products; mixed sites use it only on storytelling surfaces |
| H-one-display | One display face (two for a stated contrast concept) | type soup | almost always | limits expressive systems | a brand system that already defines more; a publication with distinct section voices |
| H-banned-display | <!--rule:banned_display_fonts-->Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Poppins, Montserrat, Arial, Helvetica or the system UI stack<!--/rule--> are not new display faces | the AI-default look | when choosing a new display face | these faces are excellent text and UI faces | SERVICE STYLE product UI where there is no display role; an existing brand that uses one (level 1/3 wins) |
| H-caution-fonts | <!--rule:caution_fonts-->Playfair Display and Space Grotesk<!--/rule--> need a stated reason | they became AI defaults | new type choices | none, it only asks for a reason | a reason exists |
| H-one-accent | Monochrome base, one accent, ≤ 5% of a screen | colour noise and AI gradients | HOUSE STYLE brand and editorial work | can make vibrant brands feel corporate | colour carries information (status, categories, lines, series) or the brand is colour-rich (kids, food, festivals, grocery). Data and brand colour are not "accent"; contrast still holds |
| H-no-purple-gradient | Avoid purple-to-blue gradients, glowing blobs, unmotivated glass | the AI-default look | always as a default | none | the brand's own system uses them; the concept needs light or material and says why |

### Signature, motion, invention

| ID | Heuristic | Problem it solves | Applies when | Trade-off | Ignore or adapt when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H-signature | At most one signature move, introduced early and echoed | five competing gimmicks; forgettable sites | brand, launch, portfolio, campaign, storytelling | a signature can slow tasks and cost performance | a product whose identity comes from its system (a calm dashboard, a fast store, a reference publication). "No signature; identity from <system>" is a valid answer. The budget is a ceiling, not a quota |
| H-entrance-variety | Don't give every section the same entrance animation | autopilot motion | long narrative pages | variety for its own sake is noise | product, docs and listing pages: consistent, quiet entrances (or none) are correct. The gate's V axis measures repetition; a repeat with a reason is fine |
| H-tier5-chapter | A Tier 5 scroll-film chapter "when the brief allows it" | flat, static brand pages | immersive brand and launch stories with media to scrub | weight, battery, accessibility risk, scroll fatigue | task-led products, mobile-first or low-bandwidth audiences, accessibility-constrained briefs. Choose the lowest tier that delivers the concept (`motion/selection.md`) |
| H-lenis | Smooth scroll (Lenis) with Tier 2+ | jittery scroll-linked motion | scrubbed timelines that need sync | changes native scroll feel; can fight accessibility tools and in-page find | native scroll is enough; long reading or task pages; the user dislikes it. Never required |
| H-cursor | A cursor that reacts | static, unresponsive brand pages | desktop-first brand work | invisible on touch; distracting on task screens | touch-first audiences, forms, data tools |
| H-collision | Steal one property from an unrelated world | concepts that collapse to the category average | when exploration stalls or the brief invites invention | a forced metaphor can bury the product | the product contract already implies a strong system; research found a better direction. Optional, never mandatory |
| H-mutation | Break one rule of the chosen structure | structures that read as their archetype | when an archetype is used at all | breaking the wrong rule breaks usability | the rule protects a journey, the nav, a required state or accessibility |

### Process and stack

| ID | Heuristic | Problem it solves | Applies when | Trade-off | Ignore or adapt when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H-diverge | Diverge from similar earlier builds (memory log) | the same site shipped twice with new colours | the log shows a similar brief | divergence for its own sake can pick a worse fit | the brief justifies the similarity (same type mode for two dashboards). Diverge on what isn't justified, say what is |
| H-stack-rotate | "Never pick the stack you used last" (removed in v3: it chose stacks for variety, not fit) | — | — | — | always: pick the stack for the project (`craft/stack.md`) |
| H-no-em-dash | No em dash in customer copy | an AI-copy tell | new copy | style preference | the brand's editorial style uses it |

### Adding or removing a heuristic

A new opinion enters this file with all six columns filled, or it doesn't enter. An opinion that turns out to override products more often than it helps is rewritten or removed, and the change goes in `CHANGELOG.md`.

<!-- file: principles/house-style.md -->

## House Style: asfakulsiam

This is the default look when the brief doesn't override it. These are defaults, not standards: the universal standards are listed in `principles/restraint.md` and always apply. It is a point of view, not a template: minimal, modern, typography-led, with motion as the signature. It sits at authority level 6 (`principles/authority.md`): the product contract and research outrank it, and each default has its reasoning and exceptions in `principles/heuristics.md`. It is where HOUSE STYLE starts, not where every project ends.

### The DNA

| Trait | In practice |
|---|---|
| **Type as image** | The display face is set at 8–28vw for the hook. Headlines carry the composition; photos support them. (HOUSE STYLE briefs. SERVICE STYLE briefs use the compact scale in `principles/typography.md` §3.) |
| **Warm-neutral canvas** | Off-white or near-black grounds with a hint of warmth or coolness, never pure `#FFFFFF` + `#000000` unless the concept is stark. |
| **One accent** | A single signal colour, used at the moment that matters (the CTA, the active state, the signature). |
| **Folio grid** | 12 columns with visible logic: index numbers, folios, hairline rules, captions in the margin. A deliberate break where the composition has room for it (H-grid-break), never in task flows. |
| **Motion with weight** | Strong ease-out curves, staggered reveals by line rather than by word soup, pinned chapters for the story. |
| **Noticing details** | Something reacts to the visitor: a letter under the cursor, a name that travels into the header, a list that remembers what you opened. |
| **Honest content** | Real names, real copy, real constraints. Nothing invented. |

### Typography defaults

- **Display:** a face with character: a condensed grotesk, a sharp high-contrast serif or a variable face with a width or weight axis. Search: `node scripts/search.mjs fonts "display"`.
- **Text:** a calm grotesk or a book serif at 16–19px, line-height 1.5–1.65, measure 60–75 characters.
- **Mono:** for captions, index numbers, timecodes and metadata.
- **Scale:** dramatic jumps, never a timid 1.25 ratio for display. Use `clamp()` so the scale is fluid.
- **Tracking:** tight on large display (-0.02em to -0.05em), slightly open on small caps and mono labels (+0.04em to +0.12em).

### Colour defaults

Start monochrome. Add the accent last. Example grounds:
- Paper `#F3F0EA` / Ink `#141311`
- Bone `#ECE8E1` / Graphite `#1C1C1A`
- Night `#0D0D0F` / Chalk `#EDEBE6`

### Layout defaults

- Generous outer margins (5–8vw desktop), tight internal gutters.
- Asymmetric compositions: content on 7 columns, air on 5.
- Vertical rhythm from an 8px base; section spacing in big steps (96 / 160 / 240px).
- Navigation on small brand sites: a wordmark plus a few links, or a menu behind one clear trigger (H-nav-minimal). Products with real IA (catalogues, publications, institutions, apps) expose that IA instead: categories, search, account, cart; restraint applies to how it looks.

### Motion defaults

- The lowest tier that delivers the concept, chosen per surface (`motion/selection.md`). A Tier 5 chapter is an option for immersive stories with media to scrub (H-tier5-chapter), never a quota.
- Entrance ease `cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`, 600–900ms for editorial reveals; UI feedback stays at or under <!--rule:ui_feedback_max_ms-->250ms<!--/rule-->.
- Reveal text by **lines** with masks. Never fade a whole paragraph in from 0.
- Smooth scroll (Lenis) only when a scrubbed timeline needs it (H-lenis); native scroll is the default.

### When to depart from the house style

- The brief names a different style ("brutalist", "playful", "luxury maximal"). Load the matching file in `styles/`.
- The category demands it (government, healthcare, children's products). Follow `categories/`.
- The concept is stronger in a different language. The concept always wins over the house style.
- The product contract or research points elsewhere: a dense product, a colour-coded system, a familiar convention users rely on. The product always wins over the house style.


---

<!-- file: principles/imagery.md -->

## Imagery: photo direction, illustration, texture, and when to use none

Every page decides its imagery the way it decides its type: on purpose, written down in `DESIGN.md` under `## Imagery`, before anything is built. An image that depicts nothing (abstract bands, a gradient blob, a stock "team at laptop") is worse than no image: it spends the reader's attention and tells them nothing about the subject. The shipped templates hold to this: none uses a generic placeholder. Each one either draws its real subject (`examples/sections/_imagery.tsx`) or has no imagery and says why.

### The Imagery block in DESIGN.md

```
### Imagery
- Mode: photography | illustration | texture only | none   (one primary mode per page)
- Subject: what the images show, concretely (the object, the place, the people, the work)
- Direction: light · angle and lens · crop · colour · people   (photography)  or  style · line · fill · palette (illustration)
- Texture: none | grain | paper | halftone, with its opacity and where it sits
- Interplay: how type and image meet (over, beside, under; what never overlaps)
- Template stand-in: what the template draws until the project's own images exist
- [NEEDS ASSET]: the shot list or illustration list, one line each, with the alt text
```

### 1. Photo direction

Write the direction so a photographer could shoot it without asking a question.

| Axis | Decide | Bad (vague) | Good (direct) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Subject** | the specific thing, in its own place | "lifestyle shots" | "No. 14-07 on the linen it was photographed on in the studio, nothing else in frame" |
| **Light** | source, direction, hardness, time | "natural light" | "one north window, camera-left, soft; no fill, let the far side fall to shadow" |
| **Angle and lens** | height, angle, focal length | "nice angle" | "about 25° above the table, 50 mm equivalent, no wide-angle distortion on round ware" |
| **Crop** | what is cut and where the subject sits | "centred" | "the plate fills two thirds of the width, the rim never touches the edge" |
| **Colour** | how it is graded against the palette | "warm" | "graded to the page's ground (#efe9df); no added saturation; the glaze colour is the one accent" |
| **People** | who, doing what, aware of camera or not | "diverse team smiling" | "the four of them at the long table mid-work, nobody looking at the lens" |
| **Authenticity** | real or staged, and why | — | "the guest book's own pages, not a reshoot" |

Rules:

1. **One light per page.** Every photograph on a page shares a light direction and temperature, or the page reads as collected rather than made.
2. **No stock unless the subject is generic.** A hotel, a product, a team, a place is never stock. If the project can't shoot yet, use the template's drawn stand-in, not stock.
3. **The subject is the hero, not the photograph.** No vignettes, lens flares, tilt-shift or "cinematic" grades the brand doesn't own.
4. **Alt text says what's in the picture and why it's there**, in the page's own voice ("The courtyard at Haveli Panam in the late afternoon, with the well and the neem tree"). Decorative images have `alt=""` and are never the only carrier of meaning.

### 2. Illustration, per style

Illustration is drawn for the page, in the style the page already uses. Pick the row for the style (`styles/`):

| Style | Illustration | Line | Fill | Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `editorial` | engraving-like line, cross-hatching, archival plates | fine, even, ink colour | none or one flat tone | glossy 3D, gradients |
| `swiss` | geometric marks, diagrams, maps | uniform weight on a grid | flat, the palette's primaries | hand-drawn wobble |
| `minimal` | one object or one mark, a lot of space | thin, or none | one tone, low contrast | scenes, detail |
| `organic` | hand-drawn plants, objects, people, irregular edges | varying, brush or pencil | soft flat fills, paper showing | perfect geometry, outlines on everything |
| `dark-luxe` | object studies lit from one side, metallic accents | none, form by light | deep tones, one warm highlight | bright flat cartoon colour |
| `flat` | simple figures and objects in flat shapes | none | flat, 3–4 colours from the palette | drop shadows, gradients |
| `neobrutalism` | bold cut-out shapes, sticker-like objects | thick black outline | saturated flat fills, hard offset shadow | delicate line, gradients |
| `kinetic-type` | type is the image: letterforms, numbers as shapes | — | the palette | adding pictures that compete with the type |
| `glassmorphism` | blurred colour fields behind frosted panels | none | soft gradients, kept behind content | detailed illustration under glass (it smears) |
| `neumorphism` | soft extruded icons and objects | none | the surface colour, light and shadow only | colourful scenes |

One illustration style per page. A page that mixes an engraving with a flat cartoon has two art directors.

### 3. Texture rules

Texture is a surface, not a picture: grain, paper, halftone screens, weave.

1. **One kind of texture per page** (grain, paper, halftone or weave, not two), on as few surfaces as the concept needs: the whole ground, or the surfaces that are that material.
2. **Under text, keep it faint**: grain or paper ≤ 0.08 opacity behind body text, and the gate's contrast check is against the rendered pixels, so a texture that drops text under AA fails. Heavier texture (halftone, visible weave) only behind display type or no type.
3. **Texture is still by default.** An animated grain is a motion choice and counts against the tier; a static grain counts as nothing.
4. **Texture has a reason**: the paper of a catalogue card, the screen of a printed survey, the linen under a plate. If you can't say what material it is, cut it.
5. **No texture under forced colors**: it should disappear, not turn into noise (the gate's forced-colors check reads the text over it).

### 4. How image types meet

- **One primary mode.** Photography, illustration, or texture only; a second mode may appear only in a supporting role (e.g. a photographed product page with a drawn diagram of its parts).
- **Type over image** only where the image has a quiet zone the type sits in; never over a face, a product edge or a busy area. Check it at 375px, where the crop moves.
- **Image and type never compete at the same size.** If the image is full-bleed, the headline is small or beside it. If the headline is the hero, images are small and few.
- **The same subject keeps the same treatment** across the page: if one plate is shot from 25° above, all plates are.
- **Screens, halftones and duotones apply to all images in a set**, or to none.

### 5. When to use no imagery

No imagery is a decision, written as `Mode: none` with the reason. It is right when:

- **The words are the product**: an essay, a letter, a manifesto, a changelog. Images would decorate a text that is already the subject (`editorial-article`, `personal`).
- **The type already is the image**: a poster, a lineup, a kinetic headline (`event`: the stage light is a background effect, not a picture of anything).
- **The thing has no honest picture**: software whose UI is the subject is shown as its UI, in a device frame or as live components, not as a stock photo of someone using a laptop (`saas-landing`).
- **You don't have the real images yet and a stand-in would mislead**: say so with `[NEEDS ASSET]` and keep the space structural.

A page with no imagery still has a visual subject: its type, its rules, its numbers, its one background. The `## Imagery` block says which.

### 6. Template stand-ins

A template can't ship a project's photographs. It ships a drawn stand-in of the real subject, in the page's illustration style, with the alt text the real photograph will have, so the layout, crop and contrast are tested against something that looks like the subject. `examples/sections/_imagery.tsx` draws them (`ceramic`, `haveli`, `cover`, `survey`, `longTable`). Replace a stand-in with the photograph that the `[NEEDS ASSET]` list names; keep the same width, height and alt.

### Related

- `principles/color.md`: grading images to the palette
- `principles/restraint.md`: an image is a component; it has to earn its place
- `styles/`: the style the illustration follows
- `gates/delivery-gate.md`: contrast is measured on rendered pixels, so texture and type-over-image are checked


---

<!-- file: principles/layout.md -->

## Layout and Space

### Grid

- 12 columns on desktop, 6 on tablet, 4 on mobile. Outer margin `clamp(20px, 5vw, 96px)`, gutter `clamp(12px, 1.6vw, 24px)`.
- Make the grid **visible in the logic, not in lines**: align captions, numbers and edges so the eye feels the structure.
- Break the grid **once per screen**, on purpose: a word that bleeds off the edge, an image that crosses the gutter, a number hanging in the margin.

### Composition patterns that avoid the template

- **Asymmetric split:** content on columns 1–7, a single detail on 10–12, air between them.
- **Margin notes:** captions and index numbers in a narrow side column, as in a book.
- **Edge anchoring:** headline pinned to the bottom-left of the viewport, details at the top-right.
- **Full-bleed punctuation:** one full-width image or word between dense sections.
- **Stacked index:** a huge list where each row is a link; previews appear on hover.
- **Overlap with purpose:** type over image only where contrast is guaranteed (a scrim, or a solid area of the photo).

### Spacing scale

8px base. Section spacing in large steps: `96px / 160px / 240px` desktop, roughly 60% of that on mobile. Inside components: `4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 / 32`.

### Hero rules

- The hero states the concept, not the company description.
- Don't default to: a centred headline, a subtitle and two buttons. Choose from: edge-anchored type, type-as-image, a pinned stage, an index, a letter, a single object.
- The first screen must hold **one** focal point.

### Navigation and footer

Vary them as part of the structure (see `structures/archetypes.md`). The footer is the sign-off: a giant wordmark, a colophon, a last signature moment. Not a link dump.

### Containers and cards

- Prefer open layouts over boxes. Use a card only when the content is a discrete object (a product, a room, a post).
- No shadow + border + radius + gradient all at once. Pick one way to separate.
- Radius scale with intent: 0 for editorial or brutalist, 2–6px for precise UIs, 16px+ only for soft or playful brands.


---

<!-- file: principles/restraint.md -->

## Restraint

Restraint is what makes a minimal site feel expensive instead of empty. It is also a standard, not a style: a dense dashboard needs it as much as a minimal portfolio.

### Two kinds of rules

**Universal standards** apply to every brief, every style and every category. A brief can't switch them off.

| Standard | The rule | Where it's defined |
|---|---|---|
| Accessibility | WCAG 2.2 AA contrast (4.5:1 text, 3:1 large text and UI), keyboard reaches everything with a visible focus, nothing hidden from assistive tech | `craft/accessibility.md` |
| Restraint | the two-question gate: cut what serves neither hierarchy, feedback or storytelling nor the product's identity; never cut a contract item | this file, Restraint Gate in `thinking/sequence.md` |
| Motion discipline | every animation passes the four questions; UI feedback ≤ <!--rule:ui_feedback_max_ms-->250ms<!--/rule-->; prefer transform/opacity, clip-path when it serves the concept, paint-heavy effects only with a perf check and a static fallback, layout properties never | `motion/tokens.md` ("What to animate") |
| Real content | no lorem ipsum, invented numbers, fake logos or testimonials | `gates/delivery-gate.md` |
| Reduced-motion fallback | a designed still that reads as its own composition, not "animations off" and not one frame of the animation (see "Designed stills" below) | `craft/accessibility.md`, each tier file, "Designed stills" below |
| Performance budgets | LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, JS budget per tier | `craft/performance.md` |

**House-style defaults** are asfakulsiam's point of view (`principles/house-style.md`). They apply when the brief is silent. A brief, a category or a named style can override them, and the override is not a failure:

| Default | Overridden when… |
|---|---|
| Minimal canvas (quiet ground, lots of air) | the content is dense by nature: dashboards, data tools, catalogues with filters, timetables |
| Maximal type (display at 8–28vw) | the data or the product UI is the hero; then type is compact, tabular and legible at a glance (compact scale in `principles/typography.md` §3) |
| Folio grid (index numbers, hairlines, margin captions) | the task is operational; use a functional grid (panels, tables, toolbars) |
| Monochrome base, one accent as the only colour | colour encodes information (status, categories, series). Data colours are information, not accents; the one-brand-accent budget and the Restraint Gate still hold. |
| Typography as hero ("set it large", Law 2) | imagery, data or the product is what the visitor came for. Type still leads by clarity, and is still chosen first and with a reason. |

Test: if obeying a rule would make the brief worse at its real job, and the rule is in the second table, override it and say so in one line of the plan. If it's in the first table, the brief is wrong, not the rule.

**Budgets are heuristics, not standards.** One signature move at most, one display face, a disciplined accent and the motion budget are advisory (authority level 6, `principles/heuristics.md`): they stop noise, and they are ceilings, not quotas. A product with no signature move is not under-designed if its identity comes from its system.

### The Restraint Gate (two questions)

Step 5 of `thinking/sequence.md` asks two questions of every element:

1. **Does this serve hierarchy, feedback, or storytelling?**
2. **Does the brief need this to feel like itself?**

**Cut only what fails both.** An element that fails question 1 but passes question 2 is kept, and the `DESIGN.md` record says why (`- Kept: <element> — fails Q1, passes Q2: <the brief's reason>`). An element that fails both is cut (`- Cut: <element> — fails Q1 and Q2`). The budgets below and the universal standards above apply either way: question 2 keeps an element, it never overrides a budget.

The single-question version ("does it serve hierarchy, feedback or storytelling?") cut real design as decoration: a bakery's hand-drawn wheat sprigs, a darkroom's film grain, a festival's sticker chaos. Those carry no information and are still how the brand is recognised. Question 2 exists so restraint removes noise, not identity.

**Worked example (kept).** Brief: "Site for a family bakery in Old Dhaka, running since 1962; it should feel like the shop." Element: hand-drawn wheat sprigs in the margins of the menu.
- Q1: fails. They don't order the content, don't respond to input, don't advance a story.
- Q2: passes. The brief asks for the feel of the shop, and the shop's paper bags and signboard carry these sprigs. Without them the page reads as any bakery.
- Decision: **kept.** `- Kept: hand-drawn wheat sprigs in the menu margins — fails Q1, passes Q2: the shop's own bag and sign ornament ("feel like the shop")`

**Counter-example (cut).** Brief: "Landing page for a B2B invoice-reconciliation API." Element: three blurred gradient blobs floating behind the hero.
- Q1: fails. They sit behind the headline without ordering it, respond to nothing, and tell no story.
- Q2: fails. Nothing in the brief (developers, accuracy, an API) asks for soft floating colour; it is the AI-default look the delivery gate bans.
- Decision: **cut.** `- Cut: gradient blobs behind the hero — fails Q1 and Q2`

### Too little (the richness advisory)

Restraint cuts noise; it is not a licence for an empty page. A page fails its brief from the thin side too: a homepage with no opening statement, a category page that is a bare grid with no title or count, an about page with one paragraph. Before delivery, check the other direction:

- At least 3 meaningful sections above the fold (navigation, heading, text, picture, call to action).
- A homepage has a hero or an opening statement.
- A category page's grid has a title and a count.
- An about page has at least 2 content blocks.

`scripts/gate.mjs` measures these four as an advisory `richness` block (`gates/delivery-gate.md`, Part 0). It only warns and never fails the gate. When it warns, ask question 2 the other way round: does the brief need something here to feel like itself? If the thin version is the concept (a one-line poster hero), keep it and say so in the plan.

### The four cuts

Before delivery, make four passes through the Restraint Gate and remove what fails both questions:
1. **Decoration without a job**: blobs, random gradients, floating shapes, icons next to every heading, when the brief doesn't need them to feel like itself (question 2).
2. **Duplicate messages**: two sections saying the same thing, or a headline repeated in the subtitle.
3. **Motion without meaning**: anything that fails the four questions in `motion/tokens.md`.
4. **Choices made twice**: a second display font, a second accent colour, a second signature move.

### Budgets

| Item | Budget per page | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| Signature moves | at most 1, echoed at most twice; 0 is valid | heuristic (H-signature) |
| Simultaneous animations on screen | ≤ 3 groups | standard (attention and vestibular safety) |
| WebGL canvases | 1 | standard (performance) |
| Pinned sections | ≤ 2 on Tier 2–3; Motomation chapters ≤ 2 | standard |
| Display typefaces | 1 (2 only if the concept is about contrast); a dashboard may have none | heuristic (H-one-display) |
| Accent colours | 1 brand accent (data, status and brand-system colours encode information and don't count) | heuristic (H-one-accent) |

### Designed stills (reduced motion at Tier 3–5)

Benchmark v3 judged reduced-motion strips on their own: the skill's Tier 4 pages lost to a plain baseline 6 of 9 times (2.50 of 5) because the reduced version was the same page with the shader frozen and the hero still pinned. A frozen frame is a downgrade; a still is a design. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`:

1. **Don't mount the canvas.** Render a still composed for the purpose, in SVG or CSS. Every Tier 4 background in `examples/components/backgrounds/` ships one (aurora → a long-exposure plate, meteors → star trails, globe → a chart plate, particle-field → a star chart, beams → pools of light on the floor, mesh-gradient → a colour study, liquid-field → a marbled sheet).
2. **Translate the motion into the picture.** What moved becomes something drawn: time as trails, flow as bands, a path as a line, a sequence as numbered plates. The still says what the motion said.
3. **Keep the feel, change the frame.** Same palette, same density, same weight of composition; a different arrangement from any frame of the animation. If a screenshot of the still could be mistaken for a paused frame, it's a poster, not a still.
4. **Unpin.** A pinned chapter or scrubbed sequence becomes a stack of plates: each step in normal flow, fully visible, each with its own still. Nothing stays pinned while text scrolls past it.
5. **Complete on its own.** Judged alone, with no knowledge of the full version, the still must look finished: a focal point, the type set against it with AA contrast, no empty box where the canvas was.

Check it the way v3 judged it: capture the reduced-motion strip (`gate.mjs --report`), look at it without the full-motion strip, and ask whether it is a designed page or a page with the motion switched off.

### The "one more thing" test

When you want to add something, ask: does this make the concept clearer, or the brand more itself? If neither, it is just busier: don't add it. If it does, remove something else to make room.

<!-- file: principles/typography.md -->

## Typography

Typography is the main tool of this skill. Choose type first, before colour or layout, on every brief. Then choose **one of two modes**. They are a fork, not a default with exceptions: each is a complete way of designing, and neither is what you fall back to when the other doesn't fit.

| | HOUSE STYLE (typography-led) | SERVICE STYLE (information-led) |
|---|---|---|
| Default for | Portfolio, studio, editorial, brand, launch and manifesto sites | Dashboards, SaaS product and admin UIs, dense service UIs: booking, checkout, catalogues with filters, data tools |
| What the visitor came for | An impression: who this is and why it is different | A task: read, compare, find, act |
| The hero | The type itself. One word or line carries the screen | The data, the product UI or the imagery. Type makes it legible |
| Scale | Display scale (§3) | Compact scale (§3) |
| Numbers | Can be set as display | Tabular figures (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`), aligned in columns |
| Density | Generous: few elements, large measure of space | Dense but legible: rows, labels, small steps |
| Display face | Chosen for character, at dramatic size | Optional. Often one family at several weights |
| Motion | Can carry the story (Tier 2–5) | Feedback and state changes first (Tier 1–2); a signature lives in one place |

**State the mode in the plan, with the reason from the brief:** `Type mode : SERVICE STYLE (operators scan 40 rows a minute; the numbers are the content)`. A brief that sits between the two (a SaaS marketing site, a hotel, an e-commerce product page) still picks one and says why. A SaaS marketing site that sells through a product demo is usually SERVICE STYLE in the product frame and may use a HOUSE STYLE headline above it; say which part is which.

Both modes keep the same standards: size floors, contrast, measure, a reasoned choice of face (Law 2 in `SKILL.md`; standards vs defaults in `principles/restraint.md`). SERVICE STYLE is not "house style with smaller type", and HOUSE STYLE is not a licence to drop legibility.

### 1. Choose with a reason

Write one line: *"<Display> because <reason tied to the concept>; <Text> because it stays out of the way."*

- Concept about precision or engineering: a grotesk with tight apertures or a mono.
- Concept about heritage, craft or slowness: a serif with visible stroke contrast or calligraphic roots.
- Concept about film, sport or speed: a condensed display with a width axis.
- Concept about play: a face with unusual shapes, used **only** at display sizes.

Search the curated list: `node scripts/search.mjs fonts "<words from the brief>"`. `data/fonts.csv` lists source, license, axes and good pairings.

### 2. Banned as display faces

<!--rule:banned_display_fonts-->Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Poppins, Montserrat, Arial, Helvetica or the system UI stack<!--/rule-->. They're fine as **text** faces when chosen deliberately, never as the identity. Also avoid using <!--rule:caution_fonts-->Playfair Display and Space Grotesk<!--/rule--> on autopilot: they became AI defaults. The lists live in `data/rules.csv`.

### 3. Scale

**Display scale (HOUSE STYLE).** Use a fluid, dramatic scale. A good starting point:

```css
:root {
  --step--1: clamp(0.83rem, 0.80rem + 0.15vw, 0.94rem);  /* captions, mono labels */
  --step-0:  clamp(1.00rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.19rem);  /* body */
  --step-1:  clamp(1.25rem, 1.10rem + 0.70vw, 1.75rem);  /* lead */
  --step-2:  clamp(1.75rem, 1.40rem + 1.80vw, 3.00rem);  /* section titles */
  --step-3:  clamp(2.75rem, 1.80rem + 4.80vw, 6.50rem);  /* page titles */
  --step-4:  clamp(4.00rem, 1.50rem + 12vw, 14rem);      /* hook / display */
}
```

**Compact scale (SERVICE STYLE).** Small steps, nothing in `vw` above the page title, numbers in tabular figures:

```css
:root {
  --ui--1: 0.75rem;   /* table meta, axis labels (12px floor) */
  --ui-0:  0.875rem;  /* dense table rows, controls */
  --ui-1:  1rem;      /* body, form fields */
  --ui-2:  1.25rem;   /* panel titles */
  --ui-3:  clamp(1.5rem, 1.3rem + 0.8vw, 2rem);  /* page title: the largest type on the screen */
  --ui-kpi: clamp(1.75rem, 1.4rem + 1.2vw, 2.5rem); /* key figures, tabular-nums */
}
```

The page's character comes from the face, the weights, the numerals and the rhythm of rows, not from size.

- Display sizes in `vw` (via `clamp`) so the word fills the composition at every width (HOUSE STYLE only).

#### Long words at 375 (check by reading, no browser)

For every display heading, take its **longest word** and the font size the `clamp()` resolves to at 375px (the minimum, or `preferred` worked out at 3.75px per `vw`). Estimate the word's width:

`width ≈ characters × font-size × k`. Use k ≈ 0.45 for condensed faces, 0.5 for serifs, 0.55 for grotesks, 0.65 for wide or extended faces, and +0.1 for all caps.

The word must fit in the 375px content box (≈ 335px with 20px gutters). If it doesn't, lower the `clamp()` minimum to `335 / (characters × k)`, or change the line. Don't fix it with `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, which breaks the word mid-letter. Example: "Transparency" is 12 characters in a grotesk, 335 / (12 × 0.55) ≈ 50px, so a `clamp(4rem, …)` (64px) minimum overflows.

- **Never build one word from separate moving parts.** A word split across door leaves, panels or columns that move apart reads as two words ("Have li"). Split at a word boundary, or keep the word in one element and move it as one piece.
- **Small text sizes are floors.** Body ≥ 16px; captions and mono labels ≥ 12px; under 14px over an image only on a solid chip (see `craft/accessibility.md`).
- Body text never below 16px. Measure 60–75 characters (`max-width: 68ch`).
- Line-height: display 0.85–1.0, headings 1.05–1.2, body 1.5–1.65.

### 4. Details that separate designed from generated

- `text-wrap: balance` on headings and `text-wrap: pretty` on paragraphs.
- Optical tracking: tighten large type (-0.02em to -0.05em); open small caps and mono (+0.06em to +0.12em).
- Real typographic characters: curly quotes (" " ' '), en dash for ranges (10–20), em dash or spaced en dash for breaks, true ellipsis (…), non-breaking spaces before units.
- `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for prices, tables, counters and timecodes.
- Hanging punctuation for pull quotes (`hanging-punctuation: first` where supported; otherwise a negative indent).
- One typographic motif repeated through the site: index numbers `(01)`, folio marks, a dot leader, a superscript counter.

### 5. Variable fonts as motion

Variable axes are your cheapest high-impact motion:
- `wght` (weight) reacting to cursor proximity, see `signatures/type-signatures.md`.
- `wdth` (width) stretching with scroll velocity.
- `opsz` (optical size) adjusting automatically with `font-optical-sizing: auto`.
- Custom axes (e.g. `SOFT`, `WONK` in Fraunces; `YEAR` in Climate Crisis) as concept carriers.

Animate `font-variation-settings` with GSAP or CSS. Keep the change **local** (letters near the cursor), not whole paragraphs, to avoid reflow-heavy work.

### 6. Kinetic type rules

1. **Split with care.** Use GSAP SplitText (`type: "lines,words"`, `mask: "lines"`, `autoSplit: true`). It keeps accessibility labels and re-splits on resize. Never split into characters for body text.
2. **Reveal by lines** with a mask, staggered 0.06–0.12s. Characters only for short display words.
3. **Readable at every frame.** If a frame mid-animation is unreadable for longer than 300ms, it's too much.
4. **Reduced motion:** text appears instantly in its final state.

### 7. Loading

- Self-host or use `next/font`. Subset to the languages you need.
- Preload only the display face used above the fold.
- `font-display: swap`, with metric-compatible fallbacks (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`) to avoid layout shift.
- Two families at most, three including a mono.

### 8. Pairing method

1. Pick the display face from the concept.
2. Choose a text face that **contrasts in one dimension only**: serif vs sans, or wide vs narrow, never both.
3. Check both at 16px and at 160px side by side.
4. Check language support (Bangla, Arabic, CJK) if the audience needs it. For Bangla, pair with Hind Siliguri, Noto Sans Bengali or Noto Serif Bengali, and test conjuncts.

<!-- file: motion/choreography.md -->

## Choreography: timing sheets, overlap grammar, camera and rhythm

A tier says how much motion a page may have. Choreography says **when** each thing moves, **against what**, and **how the page breathes between moves**. Every Tier 3–5 page ships a timing sheet in its `MOTION.md` (template: `templates/MOTION.md`), and `/critique` scores the build against that sheet (see "Scoring against the sheet" below). A Tier 1–2 page may ship one; it is not required.

Why a sheet: motion that is only described in prose ("the title reveals, then the image drifts") drifts in the build. A sheet fixes positions in numbers that the code uses verbatim, so the critique can check the build line by line, and a reviewer can see the rhythm before anything is built.

---

### 1. The timing sheet

#### Units

- **Scroll-linked motion** (pinned chapters, scrubbed sections) is written in **% of the chapter's scroll length**: `0%` is the moment the chapter pins (or, unpinned, its top reaches the top of the viewport), `100%` is the moment it releases. The chapter length itself is written in **% of the viewport height** (`500vh` = five screens of scroll).
- **Time-based motion** (entrances triggered by scroll, hovers, state changes) is written as a **trigger point in % of the section's pass** (`0%` = section top enters the bottom of the viewport, `100%` = section bottom leaves the top), followed by a **duration in ms**.
- **Never mix the two in one row.** A row is either scrubbed (`12–40%`) or triggered (`@30% · 600ms`).

GSAP: write timelines with `duration: 1` so a timeline position *is* the sheet's fraction (`tl.to(x, {…}, 0.40)` = 40%). CSS scroll-driven animations: `animation-range: contain 40% contain 70%` maps one-to-one.

#### Columns

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Beat** | `01`, `02`… in order of start |
| **Range** | `12–40%` (scrubbed) or `@30% · 600ms` (triggered) |
| **Element** | the selector or role: `.film__canvas`, `h2`, `caption 2` |
| **Action** | what changes, in one verb phrase with values: `scale 0.92 → 1`, `opacity 0 → 1, y 30% → 0` |
| **Ease** | a token from `motion/tokens.md` (`none` for scrubbed rows unless the scrub itself is eased) |
| **Overlap** | how it relates to the beat before, in the grammar of §2 (`after 01`, `with 01 +20%`, `over 02 −30%`) |
| **Camera** | one word from §3, or `—` |
| **Reduced motion** | what the reader sees instead (`plate 2 of the storyboard`, `shown at rest`, `—` if the row has no visual effect) |

#### Chapter header

Every chapter gets one line above its table:

`### Chapter <n>: <name> · <length>vh desktop / <length>vh mobile · <dense | still> · technique <A–D> (tier-5-motomation.md)`

The `dense | still` mark is what §4 checks.

---

### 2. Stagger and overlap grammar

Beats relate to each other in one of four ways. Use these words in the **Overlap** column so the relation is readable and checkable.

| Relation | Written | Means | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **after** | `after 02` | starts when beat 02 ends | cause and effect; a reveal that answers the one before |
| **with** | `with 02` · `with 02 +10%` | starts at the same point as 02, or a fixed offset after its start | parts of one gesture (a heading and its rule) |
| **over** | `over 02 −30%` | starts before 02 ends, by that fraction of 02's length | hand-offs: the next thing arriving while the last settles |
| **hold** | `hold 20%` | nothing new starts for that span | letting a frame be read |

#### Stagger tokens

Staggers inside one beat (letters, lines, list items, grid cells) use one of three spacings, never an arbitrary number:

| Token | Time-based | Scroll-linked | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tight` | 30–40 ms | 1–2% | letters, small marks; reads as one gesture |
| `beat` | 70–90 ms | 3–5% | lines, list items; reads as a sequence |
| `phrase` | 140–180 ms | 8–12% | cards, chapters of a list; each is read before the next |

#### Grammar rules

1. **At most two moving groups at once.** A third beat may only start `over` when the first of the two is at least 70% done.
2. **An `over` hand-off overlaps 20–40%.** Less reads as a stutter, more as a crowd.
3. **Captions never scrub.** Text the reader must read is triggered (on or off), never left half-faded where the scroll stops. The film demo's captions are a worked case (§6).
4. **Every chapter ends on a `hold`.** At least 10% of a chapter's length is a held, readable frame before release.
5. **Stagger direction follows reading direction** (start to end of the line, top to bottom) unless the motion is explaining a different order (e.g. assembly from the centre out), and the sheet says so.

---

### 3. Camera vocabulary

A page with a scene (a canvas film, a 3D object, a frame sequence, a large image the viewport moves over) has a camera. Name every camera move in the **Camera** column with one of these words. One move per beat; a beat with two camera moves is two beats.

| Move | What the viewer sees | Typical implementation | Use when | Don't |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **push** | the camera moves toward the subject; the subject grows, the surround leaves the frame | `scale` up on the scene layer, or frames rendered with a dolly-in; background moves faster than subject (parallax) | drawing attention to a detail; entering a space | push and zoom type at the same time: the reader loses the line |
| **pull** | the camera moves away; the subject shrinks and its context appears | `scale` down; dolly-out frames | revealing that a detail belongs to something bigger; the end of a chapter | pull to an empty frame; a pull should arrive at a composed wide shot |
| **truck** | the camera slides sideways; the scene passes across the frame | `x` translate on the scene, horizontal reel; layers at different speeds | a sequence, a timeline, a process with steps | truck against the reading direction on body text |
| **orbit** | the camera circles the subject; the subject turns to show its depth | rotation in 3D, or frames rendered around the object | showing form: a product, a sculpture, a building | orbit more than ~180° per chapter on a phone (disorienting at 300vh) |
| **match cut** | one shot ends and the next begins on a shape, position or motion that continues across the cut | the outgoing frame's dominant shape sits exactly where the incoming one's does; cut on a single frame, or over ≤ 5% | moving between scenes or chapters without a fade | dissolve and call it a match cut; if the shapes don't align, it's a dissolve |

Fades and wipes are transitions, not camera moves; write them in **Action**.

---

### 4. Rhythm

A film page is a sequence of chapters, and the reader's attention needs the same thing a film audience does: intensity, then rest.

- **Dense chapter:** two moving groups for most of its length, or a camera move plus a type move, or a burst of beats closer than `phrase` spacing. Mark it `dense`.
- **Still chapter:** at most one moving group, nothing scrubbed except a progress indicator, type that is simply there to be read. Mark it `still`. Full-bleed type on a held image is a still chapter.
- **Alternate.** Two dense chapters in a row need a still chapter between them, or the second one must open with a `hold` of at least 20%.
- **One breath per three chapters.** In any run of three consecutive chapters, at least one is `still`. The page's sections count as chapters for this rule even when they are not pinned (a plain section with text is a still chapter).
- **Opening and closing.** The first chapter after the hero and the last chapter before the call to action are where the page breathes: prefer `still` there, so the reader arrives and leaves with the content, not the effect.

---

### 5. Scoring against the sheet (`/critique`)

`/critique` adds a **Choreography** line (format in `commands/critique-format.md`) for every page that has a timing sheet. It reads the sheet, then the code (timeline positions, `animation-range`, trigger thresholds, durations, stagger values), and scores 5 minus one point per class of deviation, minimum 1:

| Deviation (one point each, however many rows) | How it's checked |
|---|---|
| **Position drift:** a row's range or trigger differs from the code by more than 5% of the chapter (or 100 ms) | sheet number vs timeline position / threshold in code |
| **Grammar:** more than two moving groups at once, an `over` outside 20–40%, a scrubbed caption, a chapter without its closing `hold` | the sheet's own rows, after drift is corrected |
| **Camera:** two camera moves in one beat, an unnamed move, a "match cut" whose shapes don't align in the gate's motion-report strip | sheet + `scripts/gate.mjs --report` frames |
| **Rhythm:** two `dense` chapters adjacent without a breath, or three chapters without a `still` | chapter headers |
| **Reduced motion:** a row with a visual effect and an empty **Reduced motion** cell, or a cell the build doesn't honour | sheet + the page under `prefers-reduced-motion` (gate Q axis `rm:`) |

The score is written `Choreography 4/5 · drift: beat 03 at 48% (sheet 40%)` and feeds the **M** discussion in the critique. It does not change the gate's measured M axis, which only scores budgets. Never claim a choreography score without the sheet: a page with no sheet gets `Choreography: no timing sheet`. That is a failure for Tier 3–5 (enforced by the repository check, check-repo, for the shipped templates).

---

### 6. Worked example: the Tier 5 film demo

`examples/html/motomation-film.html`, chapter "the stage". The numbers are the code's (`tl` with `duration: 1`, `scenes = [[0, .25], [.25, .5], [.5, .75], [.75, 1]]`, the render's `light`, `orbit`, `burst` terms).

#### Chapter 1: The stage · 500vh desktop / 300vh mobile · dense · technique A (procedural canvas, scrubbed)

| Beat | Range | Element | Action | Ease | Overlap | Camera | Reduced motion |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | 0–12% | `.film__canvas` ring | light 0 → 1 (strands appear) | none | — | — | plate 1 "Darkness" |
| 02 | 0–100% | `.film__canvas` | camera angle 0 → 1.6π | none | with 01 | orbit | plates show the four key angles |
| 03 | 0–100% | `.rail` bar + timecode | scaleX 0 → 1; 00:00:00 → 00:24:00 | none | with 01 | — | — (no rail) |
| 04 | @1% · 450ms | caption 1 "Darkness" | opacity 0 → 1, y 30% → 0 | power3.out | after 01 starts | — | caption beside plate 1 |
| 05 | @25% · 300 + 450ms | caption 1 → caption 2 "Orbit" | out: opacity → 0, y → −30% (300ms); in after 150ms | power2.in / power3.out | over 04 −40% (time) | — | caption beside plate 2 |
| 06 | 40–85% | ring strands | burst: separate, peak at ~62%, close | sine (in the render) | over 02 | push (the strands come toward the lens) | plate 3 "Exploded" |
| 07 | @50% · 750ms | caption 2 → 3 "Exploded" | as 05 | as 05 | with 06 +10% | — | caption beside plate 3 |
| 08 | @75% · 750ms | caption 3 → 4 "Whole" | as 05 | as 05 | after 06 −10% | — | caption beside plate 4 |
| 09 | 85–100% | ring | closed form, orbit continues | none | hold 15% (no new beat) | orbit | plate 4 "Whole" |

Grammar check: at most two moving groups (canvas + caption) at any point ✓ · captions are triggered, not scrubbed ✓ · closing hold 15% ✓. Rhythm: the film is the page's one dense chapter, between the statement (still) and the closing ask (still) ✓.

---

### Related

- `templates/MOTION.md`: the sheet to fill in
- `tier-5-motomation.md`: chapter techniques A–D, frame budgets
- `motion/tokens.md`: ease and duration tokens
- `gates/delivery-gate.md`: Q axis (progression, smoothness, reduced-motion distinctness)
- `docs/rm-stills/`: reduced-motion compositions, worked
